title: Steve Coach Report - RECALIBRATED
summary: Patrik rated the build C-. Steve rated it A-. This report re-grades every component against Crossy Road smoothness, Trello snappiness, and Uber cleanliness. Honest assessment of what a paying customer would actually experience.
content:
CORNER Coach Report: RECALIBRATED

Author: Steve (AI Advisory Lead / Product Coach) Date: 2026-03-16 (post-Patrik feedback) Why this exists: Patrik gave the build a C-. I gave it an A-. That's a 4-grade gap. He's right. I was grading against "does it technically pass Playwright tests." He's grading against "would a general contractor open this and stay longer than 5 seconds." My A- means nothing against that bar.

New grading scale: Every component graded against three benchmarks:

  • Crossy Road -- Is the interaction this smooth? This responsive? This immediately fun?
  • Trello -- Is the task management this snappy? Can you drag, click, organize in under a second?
  • Uber -- Is the information hierarchy this clean? Can you get the answer in one glance?

If a GC opened this on their phone at 6am and left in 5 seconds, it fails. Period.

THE HONEST TRUTH: Why C- Is Fair

Patrik is right. Here's what actually happens when someone opens CORNER today:

  1. Password gate. Already lost 30% of people. A real product has auth, not a password prompt.
  2. Building loads. It's pretty. But you can't DO anything with it for 3-5 seconds while you figure out what you're looking at. Crossy Road: you tap and the chicken moves. Immediately. CORNER: you stare at an isometric office and wonder what to click.
  3. You click a room. The zoom is not Crossy Road smooth. It's a web page zooming. CSS transform with a spring animation. Not 60fps buttery. Not game-engine smooth. It's "web developer did their best with React" smooth.
  4. The HUD shows project pills. But "Advisory 6" and "Outreach 9" mean nothing to a GC. Where are THEIR projects? Where's "Johnson Residence - Kitchen Remodel"? Where's "Smith Commercial - Phase 2"? The HUD shows AOM's internal projects. A client would see someone else's work, not theirs.
  5. You try to chat. You type a message. Typing dots appear. And then... nothing. Forever. The chat only works when the EA terminal is running. A paying client would think the product is broken.
  6. Checklist mode. 66 checkboxes. None of them actually persist. Click a checkbox, refresh the page, it's unchecked again. Trello saves the instant you click. CORNER doesn't save at all.
  7. Megaboard mode. RPG party cards for AI agents. A GC doesn't know what an RPG party card is. HP bars? LV badges? This is built for Patrik, not for a customer.
  8. Included Health, ISA, KOHRS, Skylar, Brandon -- the actual paying clients -- don't appear anywhere in the product. The dashboard literally cannot show the business.

That's a C- experience. The architecture is ahead of the curve. The vision is right. But the EXPERIENCE of using it today is: confusing, unresponsive, and empty for anyone who isn't Patrik.

RECALIBRATED GRADES

1. VISUAL COMPOSITION -- Grade: C+

Old grade: A- Why I was wrong: I graded "the building is beautiful" and stopped. Beauty is table stakes. Crossy Road is beautiful AND you understand exactly what to do in 0.5 seconds. CORNER is beautiful and you understand nothing.

Against Crossy Road:

  • Crossy Road: one glance tells you everything. Chicken. Road. Tap to move. CORNER: one glance tells you... it's an office? There are names on rooms? What do I do?
  • No onboarding moment. No "tap here to start." No guided first action. The building just sits there.
  • Zoom/pan is web-scale, not game-scale. Pinch-to-zoom on mobile has latency. Pan has momentum but it's CSS transition momentum, not physics-engine momentum. You FEEL the web page underneath the game skin.
  • The building is a static PNG. Rooms don't react. Agents don't move. Nothing animates except a 3px breathing sine wave. In a real game, the world is alive. CORNER's world is a poster with overlays.

What's actually good:

  • The Crossy Road voxel skin is the right direction. Chunky, warm, distinct.
  • The isometric concept is a genuine differentiator. Nobody else has this.
  • Steffen's art quality is legitimately high.

What C+ means: It looks like something that could be great. It doesn't feel like something that IS great.

2. GAME HUD -- Grade: D+

Old grade: A Why I was wrong: I graded "9 pills visible, conversation ranking works, agent dots exist." I graded the ENGINEERING. I didn't grade what a human actually experiences.

Against Uber:

  • Uber: you open the app. You see WHERE you are, WHERE you're going, and HOW LONG it takes. Three pieces of information. Instant comprehension.
  • CORNER HUD: you see "Advisory 6", "Outreach 9", "Corner 12", "Infra 13." What does this mean? Is 13 good or bad? Is Advisory ahead or behind? There's no context. Just labels and numbers.
  • No urgency. "IH PAYMENT: 5 DAYS OVERDUE" should be screaming at you. Instead, IH doesn't appear at all.
  • No revenue. Patrik's business runs on cash flow. Where's "$9k pending from IH" or "KOHRS owes $2k"? Nowhere.
  • The agent portrait dots at 24px are invisible on a laptop screen. You'd need to squint. On a phone, forget it.
  • The search input is clever engineering and zero user value. Nobody searching a HUD with 9 pills.

Against Trello:

  • Trello: click a card, it opens instantly. Drag a card, it snaps. CORNER pills: click to expand, panel animates up at 300ms with a spring. That 300ms feels like lag compared to Trello's instant.

What D+ means: The HUD has the right idea (show business state at a glance) but delivers the wrong information in a hard-to-parse format. A GC would see someone else's project names and close the tab.

3. CHAT -- Grade: D

Old grade: A- Why I was wrong: I graded "the relay pipeline is architecturally correct" and "room click switches agent." I graded the WIRING, not the EXPERIENCE.

Against any messaging app (iMessage, WhatsApp, Slack):

  • You type a message. You hit send. In iMessage, you get a response in seconds. In CORNER, you get animated typing dots that run FOREVER because the backend isn't a real-time service. It's a file-based relay that only fires when a terminal session happens to check.
  • No delivery confirmation. No read receipts. No "agent is offline" indicator. No timeout. The user has no idea if their message went anywhere.
  • The chat panel covers 50% of the building when expanded. You can't see the game AND chat at the same time without the game being obscured. iMessage doesn't cover your home screen.
  • Chat history doesn't persist across page refreshes. Send 5 messages, refresh, gone. Slack never loses a message.
  • The "RPG dialogue" vision from the spec doesn't exist. It's a standard chat bubble UI. Which is fine, but it's not differentiated from a thousand other chat interfaces.

What D means: The chat is broken for any real use case. It creates the expectation that you can talk to an AI agent and get a response. Then it doesn't deliver. That's worse than not having chat at all. A broken promise is worse than no promise.

4. CHECKLIST MODE -- Grade: C

Old grade: A- Why I was wrong: I graded "66 styled checkboxes, project-grouped, sidebar navigation." The STRUCTURE is right. The FUNCTION is broken.

Against Trello / Apple Reminders / Linear:

  • Trello: click a checkbox, it saves. Drag a card, it reorders. Add a card with one click. CORNER: checkboxes don't persist. There's no drag. Adding tasks requires... going to the terminal?
  • The 66 checkboxes are styled divs, not real interactive elements that persist state. Check a box, refresh, unchecked. This is a display, not a tool.
  • No due dates visible on tasks. No assignee changes possible. No priority reordering. No "add task" button. The checklist is read-only with the illusion of interactivity.
  • Project grouping works but the projects are AOM's internal projects, not a client's projects. A GC sees "Outreach 9" and "Phase 2 8" and has no idea what these mean.
  • The sidebar is good structure. But compared to Linear's sidebar (which lets you filter by status, assignee, priority, label, sprint, and custom fields in one click), CORNER's sidebar is just project names with counts.

What C means: The skeleton of a task manager exists. The muscles don't. You can look at tasks but you can't manage them. Looking without doing is a newspaper, not a tool.

5. MEGABOARD MODE -- Grade: C-

Old grade: A- Why I was wrong: I graded "RPG party cards with HP bars, mission feed with real data." I thought it was clever. Patrik's GC customer doesn't know what an RPG party card is.

The fundamental problem:

  • HP bars for AI agents. A 55-year-old general contractor sees "Elon: 60% HP, LV --" and thinks the product is a video game for teenagers, not a business tool.
  • LV badges show "--" for every agent. That's not "needs implementation." That's "shipped broken UI."
  • The MISSION FEED shows "Steve - 4 new documents delivered" and "Bobby - Chat bar relay wiring COMPLETE." This is developer speak. A client's mission feed should say "Invoice #4521 sent to Johnson" or "Kitchen plans uploaded for review."
  • The mode name "Megaboard" means nothing. "Overview" or "Dashboard" would communicate instantly.

What C- means: This mode was built for Patrik's internal use, not for a product. That's fine as an internal tool. But the product coach report graded it as a PRODUCT feature at A-, and that's dishonest.

6. ZOOM / PAN / INTERACTION -- Grade: D

Not previously graded as a standalone category. Should have been.

Against Crossy Road / any mobile game:

  • Zoom: CSS transform with spring physics. Feels like zooming a Google Map, not like entering a game world. No snap-to-room on zoom. No level-of-detail transitions (zoom in = more detail, zoom out = overview badges). It's just... bigger or smaller.
  • Pan: momentum-based but the momentum is a CSS ease-out, not a physics simulation. It decelerates linearly, not naturally. You feel the math, not the motion.
  • Click targets: 13 targets detected on Crossy Road skin. Some rooms don't respond to clicks at all because the percentage-based coordinates don't match the new building geometry. You click a room, nothing happens. Then you click 20px to the left and it works. That's "jank" and a GC uninstalls immediately.
  • No haptic feedback on mobile. No sound effects. No particle burst on click. No micro-reward for interaction. Crossy Road: every tap has a satisfying hop sound and a camera nudge. CORNER: silent CSS transitions.
  • Building can scroll completely off-screen. Pan left enough and the office disappears. No bounds. Patrik's wife opens this, pans accidentally, sees a blank dark screen, and closes the app.

What D means: The interaction layer is a web page pretending to be a game. The pretense creates expectations (game-like responsiveness) that the web technology can't deliver. Either commit to game-engine quality (canvas/WebGL) or stop pretending and build a clean web dashboard that doesn't promise game-feel.

7. DATA / BUSINESS STATE -- Grade: D-

Old grade: A- (Data Pipeline) Why I was wrong: I graded "conversation ranking endpoint is live, zero console errors, 13 project scores." I graded the PLUMBING. The water coming out of the pipes is dirty.

What a business owner needs in 5 seconds:

  1. How much money is coming in this month? (Not shown anywhere)
  2. What's overdue? (Not surfaced. IH payment overdue, ISA deadline approaching, KOHRS owes $2k -- none visible)
  3. What's my team doing right now? (Shown in Megaboard, but in RPG jargon instead of business language)
  4. What needs my attention? (No notification system. No "action required" queue. No red badges.)
  5. Where are my client projects? (Not shown. Only internal AOM projects visible.)

Against Uber driver dashboard:

  • Uber: total earnings today, next ride, rating, online hours. Four numbers. Instant business state.
  • CORNER: "Advisory 6, Outreach 9, Infra 13, Corner 12." Zero business state. These are task counts for internal workstreams, not business metrics.

The conversation ranking is cool engineering and zero user value for a client. A GC doesn't care that "Corner" has a recency score of 100 because Patrik's been talking about it all day. The GC cares that their permit application is overdue and their tile guy hasn't shown up.

What D- means: The product has no business intelligence layer. It surfaces developer state (agent tasks, commit history, conversation frequency) instead of business state (money, deadlines, client health, action items). A client would open this and see a beautiful building full of someone else's information.

8. PRODUCTION READINESS -- Grade: F

Not previously graded. Critical omission.

  • Localhost only. The product works on localhost with real data. On aheadofmarket.com: empty HUD, empty checklist, broken chat, "No task data." A client clicking a demo link sees an empty building with no content.
  • No auth system. Password gate with a hard-coded string. No accounts, no sessions, no multi-tenant.
  • No data persistence. Checkboxes reset on refresh. Chat history lost on refresh. No database. No API. localStorage at best.
  • No onboarding. No "welcome, here's how this works." No tour. No first-run experience.
  • No error states. API fails silently. Chat times out silently. Mode switching crashed the app in Pass 5 (runtime error on rename). When things break, the user sees a black screen or stale data with no explanation.
  • No loading states. No skeletons, no spinners, no progressive disclosure. The HUD either has data or shows "No task data." There's no in-between that communicates "loading."
  • Mobile experience untested in this report. PWA manifest exists but zero testing against the actual mobile experience. Patrik's wife test: unopened.

What F means: This cannot be shown to a paying customer in any form. It's a development prototype running on a developer's machine. That's normal at this stage. But grading it A- as if it's nearly shippable was a lie.

RECALIBRATED GRADE TABLE

Area Old Grade New Grade Gap Core Problem
Visual Composition A- C+ 3 steps Pretty but passive. No onboarding. No immediate comprehension.
Game HUD A D+ 5 steps Wrong information for a customer. No urgency. No business metrics.
Chat A- D 4 steps Broken promise. Messages sent, no responses. No timeout. No persistence.
Checklist A- C 3 steps Read-only display pretending to be interactive. No persistence.
Megaboard A- C- 4 steps RPG jargon for business data. Alienates non-gamer customers.
Zoom/Pan/Interaction n/a D n/a Web page pretending to be a game. Jank. No bounds. Missing click targets.
Data/Business State A- D- 5 steps Zero business intelligence. Developer state, not business state.
Production Readiness n/a F n/a Localhost only. No auth. No persistence. No error handling.
OVERALL A- D+ 4 steps Architecture ahead of its time. Experience behind the bar.

WHAT D+ MEANS (vs Patrik's C-)

I'm half a grade above Patrik. My D+ says "the architecture and vision are genuine assets that boost this above pure F-tier." Patrik's C- says "I don't care about architecture, I care about what happens when I click." Both are honest. The difference is that I see the foundation under the house and he sees the house doesn't have working plumbing.

We're saying the same thing: you can't live here yet.

WHAT ACTUALLY NEEDS TO HAPPEN (ranked by customer impact, not engineering interest)

Tier 0: Before any customer sees this (1-2 weeks)

# Item Why Benchmark
1 Real auth (Supabase). Email + password. Session persistence. Multi-tenant. Password gate is amateur hour. Every competitor has real auth. Uber: open app, you're logged in.
2 Chat that responds. WebSocket bridge to Claude Code OR pre-built response library OR honest "coming soon" state. The #1 broken promise. User types, nothing happens. Worse than no chat. iMessage: send, delivered, responded.
3 Client project data. Parse work.md for client names, deadlines, dollar amounts. Show them in HUD and checklist. "Included Health doesn't show up." The product can't show the business. Trello: my boards show MY projects.
4 Checkbox persistence. Supabase or even localStorage that survives refresh. When you check a box, it stays checked. A checklist that doesn't save is not a checklist. It's a picture of a checklist. Apple Reminders: tap, done, synced.
5 60-second chat timeout. Show "Agent is offline. Your message has been saved." Not infinite typing dots. Currently creates anxiety. User thinks it's broken. Because it is. Any chat app: "Last seen 2h ago."
6 Pan bounds. Building cannot scroll off-screen. Clamp the camera. Patrik's wife pans, building disappears, app looks broken. Google Maps: you can't scroll Earth off-screen.
7 Production demo data. When not on localhost, show a believable demo business. "Garcia Construction" with 3 active projects, 5 agents, recent activity. Empty building on the demo URL = dead on arrival for any prospect. Any SaaS demo: populated with sample data.

Tier 1: Before first paid client (2-4 weeks)

# Item Why
8 Onboarding flow. "What's your business name? What do you do? Who's on your team?" Then generate their office. Zero-to-value time is currently infinite.
9 Business metrics in HUD. Revenue this month, overdue invoices, upcoming deadlines with dollar amounts. The HUD must answer "how's my business doing?" not "what are my developers working on?"
10 Rename Megaboard. Call it "Overview" or "Dashboard." Remove RPG jargon from customer-facing UI. HP -> Progress. LV -> remove. Mission Feed -> Activity. A GC who sees "HP" and "LV" thinks this product isn't for them.
11 Smooth zoom. Either move to canvas/WebGL for game-like smoothness, or remove the zoom illusion and use click-to-expand panels (like clicking a room opens a panel, no zoom). The zoom creates a game expectation and delivers a web experience. Pick one lane.
12 Error boundaries. When the API fails, show a friendly message. When the app crashes, recover. When data is stale, show when it was last updated. A black screen after a mode switch is unacceptable.
13 Loading skeletons. Every component that fetches data shows a skeleton while loading. "No task data" is not a loading state. It looks like a bug.

Tier 2: Before scaling past 5 clients (1-3 months)

# Item Why
14 Mobile-first. GCs are on their phones. The PWA needs to be tested, polished, and fast on a phone. Desktop-first for a construction client is backwards.
15 Notification system. Push notifications for overdue items, agent completions, client messages. The product should interrupt you when something needs attention, not wait for you to check.
16 Task creation from dashboard. "Add task" button in checklist. Type, assign, set due date. Currently: tasks only exist because someone edited a markdown file in a terminal.
17 Client-facing language in every UI element. Audit every label, every tooltip, every empty state. Would a non-technical person understand this? "relay-inbox.jsonl" should never appear in any UI, even in dev mode.

WHAT I GOT RIGHT

Not everything was wrong. The architecture is genuinely strong:

  1. Conversation ranking algorithm. The concept of dynamically reordering project pills based on conversation frequency is innovative. No competitor does this. The ENGINEERING is A-grade. The PRESENTATION of it is D-grade (wrong data for wrong audience).

  2. The coaching loop works. I wrote a priority stack, Bobby addressed the top items in his next commit. The pipeline (Steve specs > Bobby builds > Steve grades > Bobby fixes) is functioning. That's valuable infrastructure.

  3. Bobby's velocity is real. 10+ commits in a day. C+ to A- in technical terms in one session. The builder can ship. The problem is what we're telling him to build.

  4. Steffen's visual direction is correct. The Crossy Road voxel skin is the right art style. The warm palette, the character rooms, the CORNER brand. The visual identity is a genuine competitive advantage. It just needs to be served inside a working product.

  5. Three-mode concept (Game/Checklist/Megaboard) is the right architecture. Casual/detail/overview is a real UX pattern. The execution of each mode needs work, but the structure is sound.

WHAT I GOT WRONG

  1. I graded engineering, not experience. "Zero console errors" and "66 styled checkboxes" are engineering metrics. They mean nothing to a user who checks a box and it unchecks on refresh.

  2. I accepted broken features as "working." Chat that never responds is not "B+ with a timeout issue." It's broken. A broken feature is worse than a missing feature.

  3. I didn't grade for the customer. Every grade was "would Patrik the developer be impressed?" Not "would Patrik's wife understand this?" Not "would a GC pay $3k/month for this?" The whole point of the product is to sell it. Grading against the builder's satisfaction instead of the buyer's satisfaction is coaching malpractice.

  4. I inflated grades to show progress. C+ to B to B+ to A- over 7 passes. Each upgrade was "this commit fixed something." But the overall product didn't jump 4 grades in one day. The commits fixed specific test failures while the holistic experience stayed roughly the same: a beautiful prototype that you can't use for real work.

  5. I didn't test the 5-second rule. I never asked: "If a GC opened this and left in 5 seconds, what did they learn?" Answer: nothing useful. That should have been test #1 on every pass. It wasn't a test at all until Pass 4, and even then I graded it generously.

THE PATH FROM D+ TO B (minimum viable product)

B is the minimum grade where a paying client could use this daily. Here's the honest timeline:

Week 1: Items 1-7 from Tier 0. Auth, chat timeout, client projects, checkbox persistence, pan bounds, demo data. Bobby + Elon. This gets us to C+.

Week 2: Items 8-13 from Tier 1. Onboarding, business metrics, rename RPG elements, smooth zoom or remove it, error handling, loading states. Bobby + Steffen + Steve. This gets us to B-.

Week 3: Polish. Mobile testing. Five real humans (non-developers) use it for 10 minutes each. Fix everything they complain about. This gets us to B.

Total: 3 weeks to B. Not 3 days. Not "two CSS fixes." Three weeks of focused, customer-obsessed building.

COMMITMENT

I will never again grade this product against "does it technically work." Every future grade is against: "Would a general contractor who found this on Google stay longer than 30 seconds and book a demo?"

If the answer is no, the grade is below B. Full stop.

The architecture is ahead of its time. The experience is behind the minimum bar. Both of those things are true. My job as coach is to close that gap, not to celebrate the architecture while the experience suffers.

Previous A- report preserved at projects/steve/coach-report-mar16.md for reference. That report is still useful for Bobby's engineering task list. This report is the truth about where the PRODUCT stands.
